Force Analysis At each radial station r, the velocity experienced by a blade element results
from vector combination of forward aircraft velocity V (or axial induced velocity for a hovering
rotor), tangential rotational velocity omega*r, and induced velocities from the rotor wake. The resultant relative
velocity V_r makes an inflow angle Phi with the rotor plane: tan(Phi) = (V +
v_i) / (omega*r - u_i) where v_i is axial induced velocity and u_i is tangential
induced velocity (swirl). The angle of attack alpha emerges from the relationship between blade geometric
pitch angle theta and the inflow path angle Phi: alpha = theta - Phi The
lift force on an element follows standard airfoil dynamics: dL = (1/2) * rho *
V_r^2 * c * C_L * dr where rho is air density, c is local
blade chord, and C_L denotes section lift coefficient (a function of angle of attack, Mach
number, and Reynolds number). The drag force takes the analogous form: dD = (1/2) *
rho * V_r^2 * c * C_D * dr Thrust dT and tangential force dF
(torque per unit radius divided by r) components are extracted through geometric decomposition using the
local inflow angle: dT = dL*cos(Phi) - dD*sin(Phi) dF = dL*sin(Phi) + dD*cos(Phi) dQ =
r * dF where dQ is the elemental torque. Integration across the span and multiplication
by the number of blades B yields total thrust T and total torque Q. ##
Efficiency Characteristics Element efficiency depends fundamentally on the ratio of forward to tangential velocity (tan
Phi) and airfoil drag-to-lift characteristics. The expression eta = tan(Phi) / tan(Phi + gamma), where
gamma = arctan(C_D/C_L), reveals that propeller efficiency maximizes at Phi = 45 degrees - gamma/2.
For airfoils with lift-to-drag ratios of approximately 28.6, maximum theoretical element efficiency reaches 0.932. Operating
angles typically encountered in practical propellers (10 degrees to 15 degrees) demonstrate heightened sensitivity to
airfoil L/D ratios. ## Integration and Performance Prediction Total propeller thrust and torque require integration
of element contributions across the blade span: T = (1/2) * rho * V^2 *
B * integral(T_c dr from 0 to R) Q = (1/2) * rho * V^2
* B * integral(Q_c dr from 0 to R) Practical calculations employ Simpson's rule or
planimetric methods to evaluate these integrals from thrust and torque grading curves plotted against radius.
In nondimensional form for propellers, one defines the thrust coefficient C_T = T / (rho
* n^2 * D^4), the torque coefficient C_Q = Q / (rho * n^2 *
D^5), the power coefficient C_P = 2*pi*C_Q, and the advance ratio J = V /
(n*D), where n is rotations per second and D is propeller diameter. Propulsive efficiency is
then eta = J * C_T / C_P. ## Critical Limitations The simple blade element
theory exhibits several inherent deficiencies. First, airfoil coefficients derive from wind tunnel tests on finite-aspect-ratio
wings (typically aspect ratio 6), yet induced flow characteristics differ substantially between isolated airfoils and
propeller blade elements operating within a cascade configuration. Pressure distribution measurements on actual propeller blades
reveal that lift coefficient of the propeller blade element differs considerably from that measured at
the same angle of attack on an airfoil of aspect ratio 6. Second, inter-blade interference
remains unmodeled. Elements at identical radii form cascades analogous to multiplanes with negative stagger; gap
effects diminish toward blade tips but intensify near roots. Third, tip losses receive no theoretical
treatment, causing calculated forces near the tip to exceed experimental measurements. ## Blade Element Momentum
Theory Blade element momentum theory (BEMT) combines BET with the momentum-conservation analysis of Rankine and
Froude, which treats the rotor as an actuator disk imparting momentum to the passing air.
For each annular control volume, the momentum theorem equates the mass flow rate times the
change in velocity to the thrust computed from blade element forces: dT = 4*pi*r*rho*(V +
v_i)*v_i * dr = rho * V_r^2 * B * c * (C_L*cos(Phi) - C_D*sin(Phi))
/ 2 * dr Similarly for torque: dQ = 4*pi*r^3*rho*(V + v_i)*u_i * dr These
coupled equations are solved iteratively for the induced velocity components at each radius. BEMT became
the standard method for wind turbine aerodynamic design, underlying codes such as NREL's AeroDyn and
WT_Perf. ## Prandtl Tip Loss Correction Ludwig Prandtl derived a correction factor to account for
the finite number of blades and the resulting non-uniform induced velocity near the tip. The
Prandtl tip loss factor F is defined as: F = (2/pi) * arccos(exp(-f)) f =
(B/2) * (R - r) / (r * sin(Phi)) where R is the rotor tip
radius. The factor F approaches 1 away from the tip and falls to 0 at
the tip, effectively reducing the thrust and torque near the blade tip to reflect the
real induced-velocity distribution. A similar correction (the Prandtl hub loss factor) is applied at the
root. ## Helicopter Rotor Applications In helicopter aerodynamics, BEMT is extended to handle the far
more complex environment of a rotor in forward flight, where each blade experiences a cyclically
varying velocity field. In forward flight, the advancing blade (on the side moving into the
freestream) sees a higher resultant velocity than the retreating blade, causing periodic variations in lift
that are reacted through blade flapping motion about the flap hinge. The cyclic pitch control
varies blade pitch with azimuth angle psi in the form theta(psi) = theta_0 + theta_1c*cos(psi)
+ theta_1s*sin(psi), enabling control of the rotor thrust vector. Tip-loss effects, compressibility (the advancing blade
tip can exceed Mach 0.9 in forward flight), dynamic stall on the retreating blade, and
reverse flow near the root all complicate rotor aerodynamics beyond the simple BEMT framework. Comprehensive
codes such as CAMRAD, FLIGHTLAB, and RCAS couple BEMT or free-wake models with structural dynamics,
trim, and control. ## Wind Turbine Aerodynamics For wind turbines, the BEMT framework is adapted
with sign conventions suited to a power-extracting rotor rather than a thrust-producing propeller. The axial
induction factor a and tangential induction factor a' characterize the induced velocities relative to freestream
and rotational speed: V_axial = V_infinity * (1 - a) V_tangential = omega*r * (1
+ a') The Betz limit of 16/27 approximately 0.593 caps the theoretical power coefficient for
an ideal actuator disk extracting energy from an unbounded flow. Modern wind turbine blades are
designed with tapered and twisted airfoil sections (NACA, DU, NREL, FFA, or Riso families) optimized
for high L/D at the design tip-speed ratio lambda = omega*R/V_infinity, typically 6-10 for modern
horizontal-axis turbines. ## Reynolds Number and Scale Effects Airfoil characteristic measurements must occur at Reynolds
numbers comparable to actual rotor operation to eliminate scale-dependent phenomena. For small rotors or wind
turbine inboard sections, low-Reynolds-number effects (laminar separation bubbles, hysteresis) become important. NASA and NACA technical
reports have documented airfoil performance across a wide Reynolds number range, enabling database construction for
BEMT codes. ## Practical Validation A benchmark analysis of a three-foot Navy-form propeller (two-bladed, pitch-diameter
ratio 0.7, operating at 40 mph and 1,800 rpm) demonstrates predictive accuracy: calculated thrust 7.42
lb versus experimental 7.77 lb (approximately 5% underestimation); calculated efficiency 0.830 versus measured 0.771 (approximately
8% overestimation). Power absorption showed greater discrepancy at 11% underprediction, illustrating the theory's sensitivity to
airfoil database selection and Reynolds number matching. The discrepancies between simple theoretical predictions and experimental
measurements underscore why a skilful designer having a knowledge of suitable empirical factors can design
propellers which usually fit the main conditions imposed upon them fairly well, though the approach
lacks sufficient precision for optimization of detailed parameters affecting efficiency. Modern design workflows supplement BEMT
with computational fluid dynamics (RANS and LES) and experimental validation, but BEMT remains the workhorse
for preliminary design and performance prediction of propellers, helicopter rotors, and wind turbines alike.
# Molecular Self-Assembly and Nanotechnology: A Technical Overview ## Core Definition and Mechanisms Molecular self-assembly
is the process by which molecules adopt a defined arrangement without guidance or management from
an outside source. Two broad categories exist: intermolecular self-assembly (multiple molecules organizing together into supramolecular
architectures) and intramolecular folding (single molecule conformational changes producing defined tertiary structures, as in protein
folding). The driving forces behind self-assembly involve non-covalent interactions. Assembly of molecules in such systems
is directed through non-covalent interactions including hydrogen bonding, metal coordination, hydrophobic forces, van der Waals
forces, pi-stacking interactions, and electrostatic interactions, as well as electromagnetic interactions. These weak but numerous
interactions create thermodynamic driving forces favoring organized structures over random distributions. Although individual non-covalent bonds
are weak (typically 1-10 kcal/mol compared to 50-100 kcal/mol for covalent bonds), the collective effect
of many cooperative interactions produces robust assemblies. Self-assembly is thermodynamically driven: the final assembled state
represents a local or global minimum of free energy. Kinetic pathways matter because many assemblies
pass through metastable intermediates, and reversible bond formation allows error correction during assembly (annealing out
misassembled configurations). ## Supramolecular Chemistry Framework Molecular self-assembly constitutes a key concept in supramolecular chemistry.
The resulting structures demonstrate remarkable diversity: a variety of different shapes and sizes can be
obtained using molecular self-assembly. Common supramolecular assemblies include colloids, biomolecular condensates, micelles, vesicles, liquid crystal
phases, and Langmuir monolayers formed by surfactant molecules at interfaces. Researchers have constructed Borromean rings—interlocking
structures where removal of one ring unlocks each of the other rings—using both DNA and
synthetic building blocks. This demonstrates the precision possible through directed molecular assembly and the ability
to produce topologically nontrivial structures by design. Other engineered supramolecular topologies include catenanes (interlocked rings)
and rotaxanes (a ring threaded on an axle with stoppers), both of which have been
incorporated into molecular machines. ## DNA Nanotechnology Applications DNA nanotechnology represents a major application domain
for self-assembly. DNA nanotechnology uses the unique molecular recognition properties of DNA and other nucleic
acids to create self-assembling branched DNA complexes with useful properties. Critically, DNA is thus used
as a structural material rather than as a carrier of biological information, to make structures
such as complex 2D and 3D lattices (both tile-based as well as using the DNA
origami method) and three-dimensional structures in the shapes of polyhedra. The DNA origami technique, introduced
by Paul Rothemund in 2006, enables programmable construction of geometric structures through careful strand design.
A long scaffold strand (typically from the M13mp18 bacteriophage genome) is folded by hundreds of
short staple strands into arbitrary two- and three-dimensional shapes with approximately 6-nanometer spatial resolution. These
DNA scaffolds serve additional functions: DNA structures have been used as templates in the assembly
of other molecules such as gold nanoparticles and streptavidin proteins, enabling hierarchical assembly of complex
nanostructures combining multiple material types. Ned Seeman's pioneering work in the 1980s laid the groundwork
by designing immobile Holliday junctions with four arms that can tile the plane. His crossover-based
DX and TX tiles enabled the construction of extended periodic lattices and programmed finite assemblies,
directly presaging tile-based molecular computation. ## Molecular Machines and Rotary Motors Molecular machines—supramolecular assemblies that
perform mechanical work in response to external stimuli—represent a frontier application of self-assembly. Examples include
light-driven molecular rotors (Feringa's motors), acid-base-switchable rotaxanes and catenanes, and protein-based machines such as ATP
synthase and bacterial flagellar motors. These artificial machines typically exploit conformational switches between stable states
triggered by pH, redox chemistry, photon absorption, or metal binding. Interlocked architectures—rotaxanes and catenanes—provide the
mechanical coupling between moving parts. ## Two-Dimensional Monolayer Self-Assembly Surface-based self-assembly produces highly ordered molecular
films. The spontaneous assembly of a single layer of molecules at interfaces is usually referred
to as two-dimensional self-assembly. Self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) of alkanethiols on gold surfaces provide a canonical
example: the sulfur head group chemisorbs to gold, while the alkyl tails interact through van
der Waals forces to form ordered, densely packed layers. Historical progress accelerated with instrumental development:
early direct proofs showing that non-surface active molecules can assemble into higher-order architectures at solid
interfaces came with the development of scanning tunneling microscopy and shortly thereafter atomic force microscopy,
which enabled real-space visualization of molecular arrangements on surfaces. Two primary strategies emerged for 2D
self-assembly: self-assembly following ultra-high-vacuum deposition and annealing, and self-assembly at the solid-liquid interface. The field
has advanced to incorporate crystal engineering at the nanoscopic scale, enabling researchers to design both
molecular components and environmental conditions to produce highly crystalline architectures with predictable properties. ## Drexler's
Engines of Creation and Molecular Nanotechnology K. Eric Drexler's 1986 book Engines of Creation articulated
a sweeping vision of molecular nanotechnology (MNT): molecular assemblers—programmable machines that could build nearly any
structure atom by atom from simple feedstocks. Drexler's vision drew directly on von Neumann's universal
constructor, proposing that mechanical molecular machines could achieve the same self-replicating, general-purpose fabrication capability in
the physical world that von Neumann had demonstrated was logically possible in cellular automaton space.
The key concepts of Drexler's framework include: the molecular assembler, a device capable of guiding
chemical reactions by positioning reactive molecules with atomic precision; mechanosynthesis, controlled chemistry through mechanical positioning
of reactants; diamondoid materials as a primary construction medium due to their strength and computational
simulability; and exponentially self-replicating assemblers as a path to bulk manufacturing. Drexler's Nanosystems (1992) provided
detailed engineering analyses of molecular gears, bearings, manipulator arms, and molecular-scale computers. While Drexler's vision
remains contested—Richard Smalley and others questioned the feasibility of mechanosynthesis with highly reactive species—components of
it have been realized experimentally. DNA-based molecular robots have been shown to pick up and
sort molecular cargo. Scanning probe lithography demonstrates atomically precise surface modification. The basic principle of
programmable self-assembly is now experimentally routine, even if universal molecular assemblers remain speculative. ## Connection
to Von Neumann's Universal Constructor Von Neumann's universal constructor, formalized in the late 1940s within
a 29-state cellular automaton, demonstrated that a machine could in principle build copies of itself
given suitable raw materials and an instruction tape describing its own construction. Molecular self-assembly research
embodies a physical-chemistry instantiation of this idea: DNA strands encode assembly instructions in their sequences,
bind through programmable Watson-Crick complementarity, and spontaneously organize into predesigned structures. Autocatalytic reaction networks in
prebiotic chemistry, self-replicating peptides (Ghadiri's work), and synthetic RNA replicators all instantiate the self-reproducing automaton
idea in real molecules. Modern DNA origami, molecular robotics, and supramolecular chemistry collectively form what
might be called the experimental realization of von Neumann's abstract vision: machines that encode their
own blueprints, assemble through local interactions, and replicate themselves from simple building blocks. ## Biological
Self-Assembly Systems Self-assembly plays fundamental roles in living systems. Molecular self-assembly underlies the construction of
biologic macromolecular assemblies and biomolecular condensates in living organisms, and so is crucial to the
function of cells. Specific examples include lipid bilayer membrane formation driven by hydrophobic effects, DNA
double helix stabilization through hydrogen bonding and pi-stacking, protein quaternary structure assembly through shape-complementary interfaces,
microtubule and actin filament polymerization, and ribosome assembly from dozens of RNA and protein components.
Notably, molecular self-assembly of incorrectly folded proteins into insoluble amyloid fibers is responsible for infectious
prion-related neurodegenerative diseases, underscoring that self-assembly processes, while generally producing functional structures, can generate pathogenic
assemblies when template information becomes corrupted. Gecko adhesion exemplifies self-assembly in structural biology: hierarchical beta-keratin
architectures (lamellae, setae, spatulae) exploit van der Waals forces at nanometer scales, enabling dry adhesion
to smooth surfaces. Bioinspired adhesive materials mimicking gecko setae demonstrate how understanding biological self-assembly enables
synthetic applications. ## Bottom-Up Nanotechnology Approaches Molecular self-assembly is an important aspect of bottom-up approaches
to nanotechnology. Using molecular self-assembly, the final (desired) structure is programmed in the shape and
functional groups of the molecules. This contrasts sharply with top-down approaches like photolithography that carve
desired structures from bulk material. Bottom-up methods potentially offer atomic precision, massive parallelism (every molecule
is a factory), and energy efficiency. In the speculative vision of molecular nanotechnology, microchips of
the future might be made by molecular self-assembly. An advantage to constructing nanostructure using molecular
self-assembly for biological materials is that they will degrade back into individual molecules that can
be broken down by the body, enabling biomedical applications such as targeted drug delivery with
biocompatible disposal. ## Conclusion Molecular self-assembly unites supramolecular chemistry, DNA nanotechnology, molecular machines, surface science,
and biology around the common principle that complex, functional structures can emerge spontaneously from properly
designed molecular building blocks. Traced intellectually to von Neumann's universal constructor and elaborated in Drexler's

# Stephen Wolfram's Classification of Cellular Automata and Computational Theory ## The Four-Class System Stephen
Wolfram's most significant contribution to cellular automaton theory emerged in the mid-1980s when he developed
a systematic classification framework dividing cellular automata into four distinct behavioral classes. This taxonomic approach
fundamentally shifted how researchers conceptualized complex systems by focusing on rule dynamics rather than specific
pattern identification. The foundational observation underlying Wolfram's classification concerns how simple local interactions between neighboring
cells produce dramatically different global behaviors. According to the framework, Class 1: Nearly all initial
patterns evolve quickly into a stable, homogeneous state. Any randomness in the initial pattern disappears.
These automata represent the simplest category, where system dynamics inevitably reach uniform equilibrium regardless of
starting configurations, essentially erasing information and complexity. Class 2 automata exhibit greater sophistication. Nearly all
initial patterns evolve quickly into stable or oscillating structures. Some of the randomness in the
initial pattern may filter out, but some remains. These systems preserve localized disturbances—perturbations introduced at
specific locations remain geographically confined rather than propagating throughout the entire grid. This bounded influence
suggests these automata possess limited computational capacity despite their structural complexity. Class 3 automata demonstrate
chaotic behavior. Nearly all initial patterns evolve in a pseudo-random or chaotic manner. Any stable
structures that appear are quickly destroyed by the surrounding noise. The system exhibits apparent randomness,
with disturbances spreading indefinitely across the cellular space. This unpredictability paradoxically constrains computational utility, as
the system's evolution becomes difficult to control or direct toward specific outcomes. Class 4 represents
the most theoretically significant category. Nearly all initial patterns evolve into structures that interact in
complex and interesting ways, with the formation of local structures that are able to survive
for long periods of time. These automata occupy an intermediate regime between order and chaos,
exhibiting neither convergence to homogeneity nor complete disorder. Wolfram conjectured that many class 4 cellular
automata, if not all, are capable of universal computation, a hypothesis later confirmed for specific
rules including Rule 110 and Conway's Game of Life. ## Computational Irreducibility and Class IV
Behavior Central to Wolfram's theoretical framework is the concept of computational irreducibility—a principle suggesting that
certain complex systems cannot be simplified into shorter computational procedures. Some cellular automata exhibit behaviors
that require simulation or observation to predict, as no shortcut calculation can determine future states
without executing the rules forward through time. This irreducibility characterizes Class 4 systems particularly, explaining
their computational richness and unpredictability. The relationship between computational irreducibility and Class IV behavior illuminates
why these automata possess universal computational capabilities. A system that cannot be algorithmically compressed necessarily
retains information about its history and can encode computations. Conversely, Class 1 and Class 2
automata exhibit computational reducibility—their eventual behaviors can be determined without complete simulation. Wolfram's Principle of
Computational Equivalence generalizes this observation, asserting that almost all processes that are not obviously simple
can be viewed as computations of equivalent sophistication. Under this principle, Class 4 cellular automata
share computational power with the most sophisticated computers, natural physical processes, and even biological systems.
## Elementary Cellular Automata and Rule 110 Wolfram's systematic investigation of one-dimensional cellular automata, termed
elementary cellular automata, provides the most thoroughly studied example of this classification scheme. The simplest
nontrivial cellular automaton would be one-dimensional, with two possible states per cell, and a cell's
neighbors defined as the adjacent cells on either side of it. With neighborhoods comprising three
cells and two possible states, exactly 256 possible rules exist, each designated by Wolfram code
numbers from zero to 255. Rule 110 exemplifies Class IV complexity. This rule, identified by
binary notation 01101110, generates neither predictable periodicity nor apparent randomness. Rule 110, like the Game
of Life, exhibits what Wolfram calls class 4 behavior, which is neither completely random nor
completely repetitive. Localized structures appear and interact in various complicated-looking ways. The computational universality of
Rule 110 was demonstrated by Matthew Cook, Wolfram's research assistant. Matthew Cook proved that some
of these structures were rich enough to support universality. This proof represents a landmark result
because Rule 110 constitutes an extraordinarily simple system—a one-dimensional automaton with only two cell states
and local neighborhoods of size three. The fact that such elementary rules suffice for universal
computation profoundly suggests that Class 4 behavior inherently correlates with computational universality. Rule 110 has
been the basis for some of the smallest universal Turing machines. ## Local Rules and
Global Complexity The emergence of sophisticated global behavior from extremely simple local rules constitutes a
fundamental observation motivating Wolfram's research program. Elementary cellular automata illustrate this principle with striking clarity:
each rule specifies only what happens to a single cell given eight possible neighborhood configurations.
Despite this minimal specification, the aggregate dynamics of millions of cells following identical rules produces
behaviors ranging from complete order to indistinguishable chaos to Class IV complexity. The gap between
rule simplicity and behavioral complexity catalyzed Wolfram's broader theoretical work. The unexpected complexity of the
behavior of these simple rules led Wolfram to suspect that complexity in nature may be
due to similar mechanisms. This conjecture connects cellular automaton theory to natural phenomena, suggesting that
biological and physical systems exhibiting substantial organization might operate according to principles similar to cellular
automata. Rule space analysis provides quantitative structure for understanding this local-to-global relationship. For elementary automata,
an elementary cellular automaton rule is specified by 8 bits, and all elementary cellular automaton
rules can be considered to sit on the vertices of the 8-dimensional unit hypercube. The
Hamming distance between rules—the number of differing bits—quantifies rule similarity. Empirical analysis reveals that class
1 rules tend to have lower number of bit-1s, thus located in one region of
the space, whereas class 3 rules tend to have higher proportion (50%) of bit-1s. Notably,
class 4 rules are located between the class 1 and class 3 rules, suggesting an
"edge of chaos" principle where maximum computational capability emerges at the boundary separating order from
disorder. ## Edge of Chaos and Langton's Lambda Christopher Langton's lambda parameter formalizes the edge
of chaos concept. Lambda measures the fraction of rule entries that map to a particular
nonzero state. As lambda increases from 0 to its maximum, the system transitions from frozen
(Class 1) through ordered (Class 2) through complex (Class 4) to chaotic (Class 3) regimes.
Class 4 behavior emerges at the phase transition between order and chaos, supporting the hypothesis
that computation most readily emerges in systems poised at this critical threshold. ## A New
Kind of Science and Broader Framework Wolfram's comprehensive treatment of these topics appeared in his
magnum opus, A New Kind of Science (2002), synthesizing decades of cellular automaton research. The
work presented cellular automata not merely as mathematical curiosities but as fundamental models for understanding
natural complexity and computation. Wolfram argued that simple rules underlie phenomena as diverse as fluid
turbulence, biological pattern formation (shells, leaves, pigmentation), financial market dynamics, and possibly fundamental physics itself.
The classification framework acknowledges important caveats. According to Wolfram, "with almost any general classification scheme
there are inevitably cases which get assigned to one class by one definition and another
class by another definition." And so it is with cellular automata: there are occasionally rules
that show some features of one class and some of another. This intellectual honesty reflects
the framework's qualitative rather than purely formal character. Subsequent research produced more rigorous classification attempts.
The Culik-Yu classification proposed formally well-defined classes, though membership in these proved undecidable—no algorithm can
definitively determine which class certain automata inhabit. This undecidability result underscores fundamental computational limitations even
in classifying computational systems themselves. ## Significance and Legacy Wolfram's classification transformed cellular automaton theory
from an obscure academic domain into a framework for understanding universal complexity. By demonstrating that
simple local rules generate diverse global phenomena, and that certain rule classes exhibit computational universality,
Wolfram established cellular automata as fundamental models worthy of serious scientific investigation. The discovery that
Rule 110 is Turing-complete—capable of simulating any computable function—vindicated the theoretical prediction that Class 4
automata possess universal capabilities, anchoring abstract classifications to concrete computational power. The Wolfram classification continues
to influence research in complex systems, artificial life, computational biology, and fundamental physics, providing a
vocabulary for discussing the emergence of computation from simple rules and the relationship between order,
chaos, and information processing in both natural and artificial systems.

THE FIRST BOOK OF OPTICKS _PART I._ My Design in this Book is not to
explain the Properties of Light by Hypotheses, but to propose and prove them by Reason
and Experiments: In order to which I shall premise the following Definitions and Axioms. _DEFINITIONS_
DEFIN. I. _By the Rays of Light I understand its least Parts, and those as
well Successive in the same Lines, as Contemporary in several Lines._ For it is manifest
that Light consists of Parts, both Successive and Contemporary; because in the same place you
may stop that which comes one moment, and let pass that which comes presently after;
and in the same time you may stop it in any one place, and let
it pass in any other. For that part of Light which is stopp'd cannot be
the same with that which is let pass. The least Light or part of Light,
which may be stopp'd alone without the rest of the Light, or propagated alone, or
do or suffer any thing alone, which the rest of the Light doth not or
suffers not, I call a Ray of Light. DEFIN. II. _Refrangibility of the Rays of
Light, is their Disposition to be refracted or turned out of their Way in passing
out of one transparent Body or Medium into another. And a greater or less Refrangibility
of Rays, is their Disposition to be turned more or less out of their Way
in like Incidences on the same Medium._ Mathematicians usually consider the Rays of Light to
be Lines reaching from the luminous Body to the Body illuminated, and the refraction of
those Rays to be the bending or breaking of those lines in their passing out

CHAP. II. _Of the Prophetic Language._ For understanding the Prophecies, we are, in the first
place, to acquaint our-selves with the figurative language of the Prophets. This language is taken
from the analogy between the world natural, and an empire or kingdom considered as a
world politic. Accordingly, the whole world natural consisting of heaven and earth, signifies the whole
world politic, consisting of thrones and people, or so much of it as is considered
in the Prophecy: and the things in that world signify the analogous things in this.
For the heavens, and the things therein, signify thrones and dignities, and those who enjoy
them; and the earth, with the things thereon, the inferior people; and the lowest parts
of the earth, called _Hades_ or Hell, the lowest or most miserable part of them.
Whence ascending towards heaven, and descending to the earth, are put for rising and falling
in power and honour: rising out of the earth, or waters, and falling into them,
for the rising up to any dignity or dominion, out of the inferior state of
the people, or falling down from the same into that inferior state; descending into the
lower parts of the earth, for descending to a very low and unhappy estate; speaking
with a faint voice out of the dust, for being in a weak and low
condition; moving from one place to another, for translation from one office, dignity, or dominion,
to another; great earthquakes, and the shaking of heaven and earth, for the shaking of
kingdoms, so as to distract or overthrow them; the creating a new heaven and earth,
and the passing away of an old one, or the beginning and end of the
world, for the rise and ruin of the body politic signified thereby. In the heavens,
the Sun and Moon are, by interpreters of dreams, put for the persons of Kings
and Queens; but in sacred Prophecy, which regards not single persons, the Sun is put
for the whole species and race of Kings, in the kingdom or kingdoms of the
world politic, shining with regal power and glory; the Moon for the body of the
common people, considered as the King's wife; the Stars for subordinate Princes and great men,
or for Bishops and Rulers of the people of God, when the Sun is Christ;
light for the glory, truth, and knowledge, wherewith great and good men shine and illuminate
others; darkness for obscurity of condition, and for error, blindness and ignorance; darkning, smiting, or
setting of the Sun, Moon, and Stars, for the ceasing of a kingdom, or for
the desolation thereof, proportional to the darkness; darkning the Sun, turning the Moon into blood,
and falling of the Stars, for the same; new Moons, for the return of a
dispersed people into a body politic or ecclesiastic. Fire and meteors refer to both heaven
and earth, and signify as follows; burning any thing with fire, is put for the
consuming thereof by war; a conflagration of the earth, or turning a country into a
lake of fire, for the consumption of a kingdom by war; the being in a
furnace, for the being in slavery under another nation; the ascending up of the smoke
of any burning thing for ever and ever, for the continuation of a conquered people
under the misery of perpetual subjection and slavery; the scorching heat of the sun, for
vexatious wars, persecutions and troubles inflicted by the King; riding on the clouds, for reigning
over much people; covering the sun with a cloud, or with smoke, for oppression of
the King by the armies of an enemy; tempestuous winds, or the motion of clouds,
for wars; thunder, or the voice of a cloud, for the voice of a multitude;
a storm of thunder, lightning, hail, and overflowing rain, for a tempest of war descending
from the heavens and clouds politic, on the heads of their enemies; rain, if not
immoderate, and dew, and living water, for the graces and doctrines of the Spirit; and
the defect of rain, for spiritual barrenness. In the earth, the dry land and congregated
waters, as a sea, a river, a flood, are put for the people of several
regions, nations, and dominions; embittering of waters, for great affliction of the people by war
and persecution; turning things into blood, for the mystical death of bodies politic, that is,
for their dissolution; the overflowing of a sea or river, for the invasion of the
earth politic, by the people of the waters; drying up of waters, for the conquest
of their regions by the earth; fountains of waters for cities, the permanent heads of
rivers politic; mountains and islands, for the cities of the earth and sea politic, with
the territories and dominions belonging to those cities; dens and rocks of mountains, for the
temples of cities; the hiding of men in those dens and rocks, for the shutting
up of Idols in their temples; houses and ships, for families, assemblies, and towns, in
the earth and sea politic; and a navy of ships of war, for an army
of that kingdom that is signified by the sea. Animals also and vegetables are put
for the people of several regions and conditions; and particularly, trees, herbs, and land animals,
for the people of the earth politic: flags, reeds, and fishes, for those of the
waters politic; birds and insects, for those of the politic heaven and earth; a forest
for a kingdom; and a wilderness for a desolate and thin people. If the world
politic, considered in prophecy, consists of many kingdoms, they are represented by as many parts
of the world natural; as the noblest by the celestial frame, and then the Moon
and Clouds are put for the common people; the less noble, by the earth, sea,
and rivers, and by the animals or vegetables, or buildings therein; and then the greater
and more powerful animals and taller trees, are put for Kings, Princes, and Nobles. And
because the whole kingdom is the body politic of the King, therefore the Sun, or
a Tree, or a Beast, or Bird, or a Man, whereby the King is represented,
is put in a large signification for the whole kingdom; and several animals, as a
Lion, a Bear, a Leopard, a Goat, according to their qualities, are put for several
kingdoms and bodies politic; and sacrificing of beasts, for slaughtering and conquering of kingdoms; and
friendship between beasts, for peace between kingdoms. Yet sometimes vegetables and animals are, by certain
